papers.title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
papers.abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
papers.abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

papers.title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
papers.abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

papers.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
papers.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

papers.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
papers.abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

papers.title: Multimodal Glymphatic Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis: Associations with Sleep and Disability
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is the waste clearance pathway in the central nervous system. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. This system is thought to be particularly active during sleep, yet the relationship between sleep metrics and MRI-derived markers of glymphatic activity has been scarcely explored. In this study, we aimed to perform a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of glymphatic function in MS and investigate its association with sleep parameters, clinical disability, disease duration and MRI-derived structural markers. The study included 22 patients (34.3{+/-}10.1 years; 16 female) with relapsing-remitting MS and 26 healthy controls (32.2{+/-}5.7 years; 18 female), all of whom underwent 3.0 Tesla MRI. Glymphatic function was assessed using diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coupling. In addition, sleep micro- and macrostructural features, clinical disability, disease duration, along with mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricular, choroid plexus volumes and lesion load were evaluated. Patients showed reduced DTI-ALPS index, though this difference became only a trend after controlling for MD. No significant group differences were observed in global BOLD signal-CSF coupling. However, in patients, the weaker coupling was associated with longer total sleep time, lower arousal index, greater disability and lateral ventricle enlargement, whereas the DTI-ALPS index showed no significant correlations with any of the measures. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that DTI-ALPS can serve as a reliable marker of glymphatic function in demyelinating diseases such as MS, where disease-related alterations in white matter microstructure can confound diffusion-based measures. In contrast, gBOLD-CSF coupling showed associations with sleep, clinical disability and structural changes in patients, despite the absence of a significant group-level difference. This finding suggests that gBOLD-CSF coupling may capture individual variability in glymphatic-related dynamics relevant to sleep and the clinical expression of MS.

papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

papers.title: Neural mechanisms of training in Brain-Computer Interface: A Biophysical modeling approach
papers.abstract: Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) is a system that translates neural activity into commands, allowing direct communication between brain and external devices. Despite its clinical application, BCIs are unable to robustly capture the intent of the subjects due to limited understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying BCI control. To address this, we introduce a biophysical linear neural mass model to investigate the associated neural mechanisms of motor imagery BCI (MI-BCI) by modulating the scale-free spectral characteristics of afferent inputs. We tailor this motor imagery neural mass model (mi-NMM) to simulate both MI and resting-state activity and apply it to a cohort of 19 healthy subjects trained over four sessions, during which magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals were simultaneously recorded. Task-dependent significant modulation of scale-free cortical dynamics reveals training-induced excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) reconfiguration during BCI training, shifting from widespread cortical to targeted sensorimotor recruitment. The modeled intra-regional E/I interaction strengths and excitatory population time constants capture condition and session-related changes in neural activation in the relevant areas of the sensorimotor cortex, where MI-related desynchronization and synchronization are associated with excitatory population time constants. Thus, these mechanistic findings provide new insights into the underlying neural mechanisms of MI-BCI, paving the way for tailored BCI training protocols.

papers.title: Phasic and tonic pain serve distinct functions during adaptive behaviour
papers.abstract: Pain drives self-protective behaviour, and evolutionary theories suggest it acts over different timescales to serve distinct functions. Whilst phasic pain provides a teaching signal to drive avoidance of new injury, tonic pain is argued to support recuperative behaviour, for instance by reducing motivational vigour. We test this hypothesis in an immersive virtual reality EEG foraging task where subjects harvested fruit in a forest: some fruit elicited brief phasic pain to the grasping hand, and this reduced choice probability. Simultaneously, tonic pressure pain to the contralateral upper arm was associated with reduced action velocities. This could be explained by a free-operant computational framework that formalises and quantifies the function of tonic and phasic pain in terms of motivational vigour and decision value. Additional analyses examined the relationship between model parameters, subjective ratings, and physiological and neural responses. Overall, the results show how tonic and phasic pain subserve distinct objective motivational functions that support harm minimisation during ongoing adaptive behaviour.

papers.title: Responses to unannounced rule changes in adults with developmental disabilities: A community-based pilot study with consumer-grade EEG
papers.abstract: Unannounced changes in rules or environments often precede challenging behavior and limit community participation for adults with developmental disabilities, yet their responses to change have rarely been quantified directly. We recruited adults with developmental disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, at a community day-service center. We administered a probabilistic reversal learning task and recorded resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) via a 14-channel wireless EEG system. Among the 12 adults who performed the task, total errors were comparable across participants (range 31-57), whereas a switch bias index, contrasting perseverative errors (persisting with the previously correct option) with regressive errors (failing to maintain the newly correct option), ranged from -0.96 to +0.91. In the 9 participants included in resting-state EEG analyses, a flatter aperiodic spectrum over the frontal cluster (preregistered, but selected as the focus post hoc) was associated with fewer switches after negative feedback ({rho} = .80) and more perseverative errors ({rho} = -.72). The preregistered parieto-occipital cluster showed the same direction ({rho} = .69, 95% confidence interval [-.11, .97], n = 8), which was opposite to the preregistered prediction. Frontal alpha peak amplitude was associated with accuracy ({rho} = .77), and the between-run reliability of resting-state measures was .82-.99. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EEG recorded in community settings can capture individual differences in how people respond to change. Field measurement that includes people with intellectual disability may help extend the evidence base for the Sustainable Development Goals of good health and well-being (SDG 3) and reduced inequalities (SDG 10).

papers.title: Retrospective attention strengthens a report-independent neural signature of visual perception
papers.abstract: Visual perception can remain modifiable after a stimulus has disappeared, but it is unknown at which processing stage a post-stimulus cue operates: on the lingering sensory trace, on the perceptual representation, or on later decision and report processes. We used masked retrospective cues to establish the behavioral effect and a Report/No-report EEG design to locate its processing stage. In Experiments 1 and 2, retrospective cues improved orientation discrimination even when masking reduced cue-location accuracy to near chance. In Experiment 3, valid cues increased EEG evidence for the target in a late interval, without the early enhancement expected from an early, additive sensory interaction. Without explicit target report, valid cues still strengthened the neural representation of the target, and a decoder trained only on no-report trials predicted trial-by-trial visibility and orientation discrimination in separate report trials, arguing against a purely report-contingent decisional account. When report was required, the cueing benefit appeared mainly in additional report-specific signals, which also predicted visibility most strongly. Retrospective attention thus strengthens a report-independent visual target representation, and explicit report can amplify this effect.

papers.title: Layer 1 NDNF interneurons form distinct subpopulations with opposite activation patterns during sleep in freely behaving mice
papers.abstract: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep facilitates memory consolidation by transferring information from the hippocampus to the neocortex. This transfer is thought to occur primarily when hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) and thalamocortical spindles are synchronized. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization remain unknown. In this study, we investigated the role of cortical layer 1 NDNF-expressing (L1 NDNF) interneurons in gating information transfer during SWR-spindle synchronization in NREM sleep. Using simultaneous cell-specific calcium imaging with a head-mounted microscope and local field potential recordings in freely moving mice, we compared the activity of L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons across vigilance states and during NREM-specific oscillations. Our findings reveal that L1 NDNF neurons form three distinct populations, assembling into cell networks tuned to specific sleep stages. REM active L1 NDNF and L2/3 neurons exhibit opposite activation patterns during spindles. While L2/3 cells are mostly inactive during SWR, NREM, and REM active L1 NDNF cells inhibit the network upon SWR onset depending on their coupling with spindles. L1 NDNF neurons mediate slow inhibition primarily via GABAB receptors. Systemic application of a GABAB receptor antagonist resulted in decreased neuronal coupling of pyramidal cells but did not change the inhibitory responses during SWRs. Overall, these findings highlight the potential role of L1 NDNF neuron-mediated inhibition in the response to synchronized sleep oscillations, with potential implications for memory consolidation.

papers.title: Enhancement of gut-microbiome-based classification of prodromal Parkinson's Disease cases by hyperparameter tuning, integration of multimodal data, and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is often preceded by a prodromal phase marked by non-motor symptoms such as REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder (RBD), gastrointestinal dysfunction, and olfactory impairment. Mounting evidence implicates gut microbiota in the early pathophysiology of PD. In this study, we aimed to enhance the classification of prodromal PD using gut microbiota profiles, with a focus on model performance and biomarker identification. Publicly available gut microbiome datasets of individuals with RBD and healthy controls were analyzed. Following batch correction and genus-level filtering, we identified six taxa significantly depleted in both RBD and PD groups, all belonging to short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera. Hyperparameter tuning on the testing set achieved an AUC of 0.889. When combining microbial and clinical features, the model achieved a peak mean AUC of 0.917. Feature selection identified 11 top-ranked features, yielding an AUC of 0.849. Using only the six differentially abundant SCFA-producing taxa, the model retained a strong predictive capacity with a mean AUC of 0.853. These results demonstrate the utility of gut microbiota, particularly SCFA-producing taxa, in the early identification of prodromal PD. Integration with select clinical features further improves model performance, supporting their potential role in early diagnostic frameworks.

papers.title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
papers.abstract: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.

papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: Selection vs. integration task demands shape the similarity of information neural coding
papers.abstract: Attention is a function that enables selection and integration of multiple sources of information. However, how these demands influence neural coding of information is not well understood. In this study we used EEG to examine how the selection vs. integration of stimuli shapes the content and geometry reflected on neural patterns, during both preparation and target processing. Participants performed a size judgement task in a cue-target paradigm that, depending on the block, required judging either the size of a selected item and ignoring the additional stimulus or integrating both to respond. Decoding analyses showed that under selection demands, categorical templates of the cued stimulus were active during preparation and target coding, contrasting with integration, where patterns linked to the cued category could be observed only during preparation. Notably, RSA suggested specific exemplar encoding during its processing, which was sustained also across the post-stimulus window during selection, yet was not observable under integration contexts. Our results also suggest that attentional demands shape the similarity between stimulus categories by increasing the distance between selected stimuli and distractors or by reducing it between to-be-integrated information. Overall, this study uncovers the dynamics of stimulus encoding under selection and integration demands, offering crucial advances to understand how top-down processes shape information representation in the human brain.

papers.title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
papers.abstract: Background: Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored. Objectives: We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8-13 Hz), and beta power (13-30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse. Results: Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions. Conclusions: These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

papers.title: Alpha-range neural oscillations are associated with multiple dynamic brain networks
papers.abstract: We asked whether alpha range (8-12 Hz) EEG neural oscillations, a robust indicator of cortical excitability, are associated with dynamic BOLD brain networks. Two independent EEG-fMRI resting-state datasets (discovery: n = 94 and replication: n = 33) show that low- and high-alpha periods are associated with dynamic BOLD coactivation patterns (dCAPS) involving multiple dynamic networks rather than a single static network. Unique BOLD dCAPs consisting of visual cortex activation along with sensorimotor and attention networks in addition to the posterior thalamus, were mainly associated with periods of low-alpha power. However, overlapping BOLD dCAPs consisting of default, control, and attention networks were associated with periods of both low- and high-alpha power. The results suggest low-alpha dCAPS contain unique temporal-dependent configurations related to visual, sensorimotor, and attention networks while both low- and high-alpha dCAPs consist of overlapping temporal-dependent configurations involving CON, DMN, and attention networks involved in internal and external cognition. These findings reconcile discrepancies across static connectivity EEG-fMRI findings by showing that distinct transient BOLD configurations are associated with similar patterns of alpha EEG modulation in visual cortex, providing a dynamic framework for the gating function of alpha oscillations.

papers.title: NeuroPilot: Longitudinal intravital neural imaging across scales and modalities through an agentic platform
papers.abstract: Longitudinal intravital imaging is essential for understanding how neural populations evolve across behavioral states, yet converting large-scale recordings into biological insight remains a fundamental challenge because neural signals are degraded by noise, non-rigid motion, and heterogeneous recording conditions. Here we introduce NeuroPilot, an agentic framework that transforms neural imaging analysis into a closed-loop, context-aware process, integrating a multimodal large language model with callable computational imaging modules to adaptively coordinate workflows from raw recordings to population-level readouts. Across heterogeneous imaging and experimental regimes, NeuroPilot restores motion-degraded recordings and supports consistent neural signal recovery, detection, and tracking in challenging deep-brain, freely moving, and longitudinal settings. These enable neuronal population tracking across spinal stimulation paradigms, deep-brain imaging, and continuous 24-hour mPFC recordings aligned with spontaneous sleep-wake behavior. By converting heterogeneous intravital recordings into stable population activity maps, NeuroPilot supports behavioral decoding and reveals structured neural dynamics across behavioral states and transitions. NeuroPilot establishes a scalable agentic paradigm for neural imaging analysis, expanding experimental access to the measurement, visualization, and interpretation of neural population activity.

papers.title: Artefact-free EEG during temporal interference stimulation reveals phase-specific modulation of the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Background: Temporal interference (TI) stimulation applies kHz electric fields whose envelope is modulated at a difference frequency ({Delta}f), allowing non-invasive deep-brain targeting. Measuring the neural response during stimulation with EEG is essential for establishing mechanisms and for closed-loop control. However, non-linearities in the recording chain mix the kHz carriers, producing an artefact at exactly {Delta}f. Objectives: To establish a method for recording EEG during TI without the {Delta}f artefact, and to test whether TI modulates neural activity at {Delta}f. Methods: A front-end analogue low-pass filter (7th order; 90 Hz cut-off; [≥]130 dB attenuation at 1 kHz) was bench-tested. In 22 healthy participants, residual artefact was assessed per recording with a two-stage detection pipeline in stimulation-only blocks. TI targeted the right primary visual cortex at 10 or 15.5 Hz, in-phase or anti-phase with multi-frequency photic stimulation (4.5, 10, 15.5 Hz), during a choice reaction time task. Results: The filter suppressed the {Delta}f artefact below the noise floor on a resistive load. In vivo, residual artefact was confirmed in two participants and could not be excluded in two more; all four were excluded from EEG analyses. Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) amplitude at 11, 14.5 and 15.5 Hz predicted faster responses. In-phase 15.5 Hz TI increased SSVEP amplitude at 14.5 and 15.5 Hz and shortened response times relative to both sham and anti-phase TI, which did not differ from sham. Conclusions: With front-end filtering and per-recording verification, EEG can measure TI neuromodulation during stimulation and at {Delta}f, revealing phase-specific modulation of visual entrainment linked to behaviour.

papers.title: Phasic pupil responses to melanopsin- and cone-directed stimulation remain stable across circadian time
papers.abstract: Human pupil responses vary with time of day, but whether this reflects circadian modulation of specific photoreceptor pathways is unclear. Twelve healthy adults completed repeated pupillometry during a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake protocol that limited sustained wakefulness; data from eight met the quality-control criteria and were analysed. This design was intended to limit progressive accumulation of homeostatic sleep pressure across sampled circadian phase. During wake episodes, 0.4-Hz silent-substitution stimuli targeted broadband flux, melanopsin, luminance, L-M cone-opponent, or S-cone pathways. Salivary melatonin provided participant-specific period estimates. We separated slow tonic constriction from phasic pupil tracking and compared hierarchical circadian cosinor models with constant-level models. Constant-level models were favoured for phasic amplitude in all five conditions (log10 BF10 = -3.36 to -1.10). They were also favoured for tonic minimum in four conditions; L-M favoured the circadian model (log10 BF10 = 0.67), but the evidence was imprecise. Under the tested contrast, adaptation, and frequency, these data do not support circadian modulation of phasic photoreceptor-directed pupil tracking. Other metrics and smaller or non-sinusoidal effects remain possible.

papers.title: Innate Immune Correlates of Sickness-Like Depressive Symptoms in Breast Cancer Survivors
papers.abstract: Background: Research supports immune pathways of depression characterized by sickness-like symptoms (e.g., appetite changes, low energy, sleep disturbance, difficulty initiating activity, concentration difficulties), with limited evidence for negative affect symptoms (e.g., depressed mood, feeling of failure). However, most findings come from otherwise healthy individuals, limiting generalizability to medical populations. This study leveraged breast cancer as a disease context, given the lasting cancer- and treatment-related effects on immune function, to examine the hypothesis that proinflammatory gene expression relates more strongly to sickness-like than negative affect symptoms. Methods: Data were drawn from 175 women with Stage 0-III breast cancer (Mage=55.3 years) assessed at five time points from diagnosis through 18 months post-treatment. Depressive symptom dimensions were assessed using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell gene expression was assessed using RNA sequencing-based transcriptional profiling. Primary analyses focused on proinflammatory gene expression. Exploratory analyses examined Type-I interferon gene expression and transcript-derived cell-type composition (myeloid-to-lymphoid and classical-to-non-classical monocyte ratios). Results: Longitudinal mixed-effects models across repeated assessment revealed that greater sickness-like symptom severity was associated with elevated proinflammatory gene expression (p<.001), Type-I Interferon antiviral gene expression (p<.001), myeloid cell abundance (p<.001), and particularly non-classical monocytes (p=.002). By contrast, negative affect symptoms showed weaker, null, or opposite associations. Conclusions: Sickness-like and negative affect symptoms show divergent associations with innate immune system activation and myeloid lineage bias. Results may inform more targeted interventions for both physical/energetic and psychological symptoms in breast cancer survivors, and may be relevant to other depression and medical contexts.
